claim: Biomolecular condensates composed of multiple components often separate into two or even more phases since the components within the condensate are also immiscible with each other.
source: Among them, biomolecular condensates composed of multiple components often separate into two or even more phases since the components within the condensate are also immiscible with each other (Banani et al., 2017; Hyman et al., 2014; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Banani et al., 2017; Hyman et al., 2014; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017

claim: Condensates with multiple phases can have a variety of morphologies such as core-shell or nested structures.
source: Condensates with multiple phases can have a variety of morphologies (Kaur et al., 2021; Lafontaine et al., 2021; Latham and Zhang, 2022; Stoecklin and Kedersha, 2013), such as core-shell or nested structures in which one phase is completely enveloped by the other, as that formed by the FC, DFC, and GC components of the eukaryotic nucleolus (Lafontaine et al., 2021), or structures in which droplets share boundaries and contact each other partially, as in the relationship between P-bodies and stress granules (Stoecklin and Kedersha, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaur et al., 2021; Lafontaine et al., 2021; Latham and Zhang, 2022; Stoecklin and Kedersha, 2013

claim: Multiphase morphologies serve as complex partitioning structures within the cell and are closely related to the condensate's function as an organelle.
source: These multiphase morphologies have been found to serve as a rather complex partitioning structure within the cell and are closely related to the condensate's function as an organelle, as they can control biochemical reactions through the compartment by regulating or buffering the concentration of biomolecules (Alberti et al., 2019; Banani et al., 2017; Conti and Oppikofer, 2022; Lyon et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alberti et al., 2019; Banani et al., 2017; Conti and Oppikofer, 2022; Lyon et al., 2021

claim: The morphology of the condensate is innately programmed into its constituent molecules themselves via sequences.
source: Apart from macroscopic factors such as temperature, pH, and salt concentration, the morphology of the condensate is innately programmed into its constituent molecules themselves via sequences (Lin et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2017

claim: A major driving force of liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is the attraction between molecules, which can be often achieved by interactions between intrinsically disordered regions or by multivalent domain-wise interactions.
source: A major driving force of liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) is the attraction between molecules, which can be often achieved by interactions between intrinsically disordered regions or by multivalent domain-wise interactions (Li et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018

claim: Condensates caused by associative phase separation move more inward into the phase as the constituent molecules have a higher valency.
source: Condensates caused by associative phase separation are known to move more inward into the phase as the constituent molecules have a higher valency (Chew et al., 2023; Espinosa et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chew et al., 2023; Espinosa et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021

claim: Repulsive excluded volume effects can lead to a segregative phase separation by entropic effects.

claim: Under crowded environments, excluded volume interactions alone can separate the phase with respect to the volume; the smaller ones move inwards and the larger ones move outwards.

evidence: Supported by citations to Hu et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2017
